chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Ibn Bukayr, who said:

Zurara asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the prayer in the fur of foxes, weasels, squirrels, and others of the hairy animals. So he brought out a book, claiming it was a dictation of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), that the prayer in the fur of anything whose eating is prohibited is invalid; so the prayer in its fur, hair, skin, urine, dung, and milk, and everything from it is invalid, that prayer is not accepted until you pray in something else from what Allah has permitted its consumption.

Then he said: O Zurara, this is from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), so memorize that, O Zurara. If it is from what its flesh is eaten, then the prayer in its fur, urine, hair, dung, milk, and everything from it is permissible, when you know that it is pure, having been purified by slaughter. If it is other than that, from what you have been forbidden to eat and its eating is prohibited upon you, then the prayer in everything from it is invalid, whether it was purified by slaughter or not purified.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on praying in the fur or skin of animals with haram meat versus halal meat?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated by Zurara from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), establishes a clear jurisprudential link between the permissibility of consuming an animal's meat and the validity of prayer on its parts, a principle rooted in the concept of *najasa* (impurity). It distinguishes between animals whose meat is halal (requiring proper slaughter for purity) and those whose meat is haram (rendering all their parts impure regardless of slaughter), reflecting the Shia emphasis on the holistic purity of the worshipper's attire. The narration underscores the practical implication that the ritual validity of salat is contingent upon the specific legal status of the material used, ensuring the worshipper remains in a state of ritual cleanliness.
